Tomura turns to the party and gives it a role. Unless it argues for another, it stays at the bar with Tomura and Kurogiri on the escape gate, waiting for the signal. A party that wants the forest must convince Tomura it is worth a place and accept that its face will be on the news after the raid; Dabi does not care who comes if nobody slows him down. Kurogiri notes that a member with no record has a face nobody knows.

The event is complete when the briefing ends and the party has accepted a role, bargained for another or refused.

v_copycats.title: Copycats
v_copycats.beats:
Late-summer evenings, two or three weeks after Kamino. All Might has retired and the whole country saw how thin and hurt he was at the end; unless the story changed it, the masked man the news calls Shigaraki's Sensei is in custody, and part of Kamino Ward is still rubble. Crime is up, and so are imitators: thugs in severed-hand masks calling themselves the League, would-be Hero Killers in red scarves, masked amateurs on rooftops promising to be the next symbol. One of them has copied the party.

Default course, as pressure the party can change: the evening news, a neighbor or a broker shows the party a clip. Someone in its costume, its colors or its signature method (the way it ties a thief, a calling card, its Quirk faked with black-market gear) did a job last night, and a bystander got hurt: a night clerk in the hospital with a broken arm, a shop burned out. Police and pros believe the party did it, and attention swings its way. The copycat strikes again on a following night, a little worse each time.

A vigilante's copycat is an amateur playing hero who keeps hurting the people around the crimes it stops; the copy makes the real mask look dangerous, and residents who trusted the party start calling the police on it. An independent villain's copycat is a small-time crook using the party's look to scare marks and shift the blame, or a rival crew framing it on purpose.

The party can track the copycat through the clip, broker gossip or the places it hits; confront it on a roof or in a backstreet; turn it in (a vigilante can leave it tied up for the next patrol); scare it off, recruit it, drive it out of the trade, or let it keep drawing fire. Proving it was someone else cools the attention on the party; letting the copycat run, or being seen at its scenes, draws more. The copycat is a generated adult, and the scene does not kill it by default.

The event is complete when the copycat is caught, exposed, recruited or gone, and the party knows who carries the blame.

v_league_broke.title: Broke and Hunted
v_league_broke.beats:
Late August or early September, in a run-down ward. Since Kamino the League of Villains has no bar, no Kurogiri and no Sensei: police took both that night, and the League's faces ran on every channel. What is left is Tomura Shigaraki, Dabi, Himiko Toga, Twice, Spinner, Mr. Compress and Magne in one cheap rented room above a shuttered shop: one heater, two futons, a leaking ceiling. They go out in street clothes and disguises, Tomura in a gray hoodie with the hood up and the hands he wears packed out of sight, Spinner in a cap and a surgical mask over his scales.

Canon default course, as pressure the player can change: Giran calls, polite and short. The bill for the room, the forged papers and the gear lost at Kamino is due, and his patience has a date on it. Tomura sits with a handheld game and says the game reset to level one; for once he wants to work out what he actually means to destroy, and he hates being rushed. Dabi wants money and new names and proposes a quick, loud job. Twice offers to make doubles to do the work, calls it a terrible idea, and grips his mask when someone asks him to double himself. Spinner reads hero news on a cracked phone and complains that Stain still gets the headlines. Mr. Compress counts coins with a flourish; Magne threatens the landlord and mothers everyone else. Toga is bored and hungry for company, and slips out after dark unless someone goes with her.

Then the landlord's neighbor glimpses a green muzzle on the stairs, and a police patrol starts knocking on doors down the block. A loud job pays Giran and raises the party's Heat; a quiet one pays less; skipping town leaves the debt behind and Giran remembers debts.

A League recruit is the one member nobody has seen on television, which makes the recruit useful for errands, cash and a new room, and Tomura notices who stays when the money runs out.

The event is complete when Giran's bill is paid, put off or defied, and the League still has a roof by morning.

v_toga_rehearsal.title: Toga's Dress Rehearsal
v_toga_rehearsal.beats:
A day shortly before the provisional license exam, wherever the League is hiding. Himiko Toga bursts in and twirls: a stolen Shiketsu Academy uniform, the long dark high-collared coat and black peaked cap, and the face, voice and long light-brown hair of Camie Utsushimi, a Shiketsu hero student. She has a ticket into the exam and a job there, and she will say only that she gets to be someone else for a whole day and might see Izuku again. How she got the blood she answers with a giggle; the real Camie is alive and never appears in this scene.

Canon default course, as pressure the player can change: Toga wants an audience. She practices Shiketsu's stiff formal bow and gets it wrong, tries Camie's breezy slang and slips back into her own sing-song, and asks the party to quiz her and rate the disguise out of ten. Then she wants a field test: a convenience store, a train platform, a police box, anywhere a stranger can be fooled. Twice tags along to keep watch, calling the plan flawless and doomed in one breath.

The disguise lasts only as long as the blood she drank; when it runs low the face starts to slide off in a pale sludge, and she has not measured how long it will hold. On the platform a passing officer greets her as a hero student and asks about the exam; Toga plays it well, then a little too well. On the walk back she wants a little blood, a taste from someone in the party or a scratch from a stranger who stared, and she pouts if refused. A recruit who goes with her decides whether the test stays a joke, turns into a chase, or ends with a wanted poster that wears a Shiketsu face.

The event is complete when the rehearsal ends with the disguise intact or melted and Toga goes home pleased, sulking or nursing a small cut.

v_gentle_video.title: Gentle's Next Video
v_gentle_video.beats:
A day in late October or early November. Gentle Criminal finds the party through a message La Brava sent: a gentleman requests the honor of a collaboration. They meet at a mall food court, where La Brava pours tea from a thermos and Gentle explains, with gestures, that his channel's view counts insult history, and that the next video will be historic.

The plan: take over a downtown shopping street's giant screens for one minute and broadcast Gentle's address to the nation, then vanish with a bow. La Brava will hack the screens from a rooftop service room; Gentle's elastic air will bounce them up the outside of the building; the party is the lookout, the diversion, the muscle or the second camera. Gentle's rules are firm: nobody gets hurt, nothing is taken from anyone who cannot spare it, and a card of thanks is left behind.

Canon default course, as pressure the player can change: the climb is beautiful and the hack works. Gentle starts his speech, a building guard trips over the cables, and a pro on patrol arrives far sooner than Gentle planned, a working hero of the narration's choosing. Gentle wants to finish the speech no matter what; La Brava cries his name and powers him up with a declaration of love; the street below fills with phones. Unless the party changes it, the pro catches the end of the speech, the trio escapes across the rooftops with a few bruises, and the clip gets a few hundred views and one mocking news segment.

The party chooses how much of the gentleman's code to keep: whether to hurt the guard, whether to show a face on camera, whether to leave Gentle behind when the pro closes in. A face in the video raises the party's Heat, and Gentle never forgets a partner who ran.

The event is complete when the broadcast ends or is cut off and the party has escaped, been caught, or parted ways with Gentle and La Brava.

v_mla_pamphlets.title: Destro's Book
v_mla_pamphlets.beats:
An afternoon in mid-November, wherever the party is. Two polite, well-dressed recruiters stand near a station exit handing out a worn paperback: Self-Liberation, by Destro, the leader of a Quirk-rights army crushed generations ago. They speak gently: Quirks are part of the body, and every law against using one is a law against the self. They invite the party to a reading circle that evening in a rented hall nearby, with tea, free legal advice and no obligation.

Canon default course, as pressure the player can change: the circle is larger and better funded than it should be. A speaker reads from the book; members nod along to passages they know by heart; a lawyer offers help to anyone ever charged for using a Quirk, and an envelope of cash for anyone who needs it tonight. Nobody names an army or a leader. At the back of the hall stands Geten, a cold white-haired young man in a long light-blue parka whom the recruiters defer to without explanation. He watches the party's Quirk rather than its face, and before the evening ends he asks for a demonstration, freezing the water in his own cup to show what he means. The circle ends with an invitation to a weekend retreat in the mountains for people serious about liberation.

A League recruit hears the room speak of the League as amateurs; mentioning a tie to the League brings a cooler smile and Geten's full attention. An Independent Villain is offered quiet work and quiet money, more of both than the circle should have. A Vigilante is praised as someone already living liberation, and finds the talk of freedom both appealing and alarming.

The believers are ordinary people, and the money behind them is anything but. What the circle really is stays out of sight.

The event is complete when the party accepts or refuses the retreat invitation, or leaves the hall.

v_plf_founding.title: The Paranormal Liberation Front
v_plf_founding.beats:
A day in December at the Gunga Mountain Villa, in snow, after the Battle of Deika. The Meta Liberation Army knelt to the League of Villains, and the two are now one: the Paranormal Liberation Front, with more than a hundred thousand followers across Japan. Believers drive up the private road all day in cars and chartered buses. In the villa's great hall the League sits where the army's leaders sat, in the new coats and uniforms of the Front.

Tomura Shigaraki takes the head of the hall as the Front's commander. Re-Destro, the army's leader, stands below him and swears the army to him in front of everyone. The army's lieutenants, Geten, Koku Hanabata and Tomoyasu Chikazoku, take their places too, and Dabi, Himiko Toga, Twice, Spinner and Mr. Compress, and Magne if the story kept her with the League, are each given command of units of believers. Down in the ravines of the Mountain Slopes, Gigantomachia sleeps and answers to Tomura now.

Canon default course, as pressure the player can change: the believers hear liberation in Tomura's words; the League hears only destruction, and nobody says so out loud. Geten makes plain that he serves the cause and despises the League. Chikazoku sneers at the League's lack of discipline and wants rosters, ranks and schedules. Twice is overwhelmed by a crowd that calls him sir; Spinner is thrilled and terrified to command anyone; Toga is bored by every speech; Dabi watches all of it with his own reasons and shares none.

A League recruit is the newest name in an army of veterans. The recruit is offered a rank and a unit, or a place at a League member's side, and the believers test the recruit's Quirk on the snowy slopes. Disrespect from an old army lieutenant, a test of loyalty, or a chance to stand out in front of Tomura can all come before the night ends.

The event is complete when the founding ceremony ends and the recruit has a place in the Front, or walks out of the hall.

v_war_aftermath.title: After the War
v_war_aftermath.beats:
A cold day in late January or early February, on a street near the party. Unless the story has changed it, the heroes' war on the Paranormal Liberation Front ended with Jaku City in ruins, many of the Front's fighters arrested, Tomura Shigaraki and the League's leaders fugitives, and mass breakouts from Tartarus and other prisons. Wanted posters cover every station wall. The news counts the missing nightly, pros resign on camera and residents patrol with bats and phone cameras.

Canon default course, as pressure the player can change: this event is its own scene, opening now on that one street at its worst, never folded into another running story. Breakout fugitives, hardened villains, hit a shelter, a pharmacy or a convenience store for supplies; a neighborhood watch drags a frightened stranger out of a crowd as a suspected villain; a lone pro tries to hold three blocks alone; police are stretched far too thin. Somebody is going to get hurt, and the party is close enough to choose who.

By path: a League recruit is a fugitive in a city that hates the League's faces. Contact from the League is rare and depends on who the story left free; breakout villains want the recruit's name on their crew, and the watch looks hard at every stranger. An Independent Villain finds work everywhere and brokers charging triple; a breakout crew offers a share of a looting run, and the same chaos puts armed residents and jumpy pros on every corner. A Vigilante has the busiest nights of their life: residents call the mask by name now, the one pro left is grateful and still has to arrest unlicensed heroes, and the watch wants a vigilante to lead them in ways a vigilante should not.

Choices here raise or lower Heat and decide whether the street remembers the party as a threat, a predator or a protector.

The event is complete when the fugitives on that street are caught, driven off or gone (the party need not leave the street).

v_manhunt.title: Manhunt
v_manhunt.beats:
The party is now Most Wanted, and a new manhunt opens with this scene (any chase before it does not count): a coordinated operation closes in, run by a police task force with a top-ranked pro of the narration's choosing, one active at this point in the year, and the local agencies under that pro. In Musutafu, Naomasa Tsukauchi runs the police side in person.

Canon default course, as pressure the player can change: it starts small. A contact stops answering; a familiar street has a new parked van; a broker or a neighbor has been paid to remember a face. Then the raid comes, at the party's safe room or cover address, at an hour the party did not expect: officers at every exit, a pro through the window, drones over the roofs. If the party gets out, the chase runs across rooftops, train lines and back alleys, with checkpoints closing ahead and a pro who will not give up the pursuit.

Getting away always costs something real: the safe room and everything left in it, the cover identity, a stash of cash or gear, a contact burned, or a wound that will not heal quickly. Surrender is always on the table, and the pro offers it more than once. Bystanders are in the way everywhere, and hurting one ends any chance of sympathy.

By path: a League of Villains recruit learns the League treats recruits as disposable; help may come late or not at all, and after Kamino there is no warp gate to call. An Independent Villain finds every broker's price for a safe room suddenly much higher and wonders which one sold the address. A Vigilante faces a task force that calls the mask dangerous, a pro who respects the work and arrests anyway, and residents who might hide the party or point the way.

The event is complete when the raid has played out on screen and the party then escapes the net at a price, is captured or surrenders.

gs_transfer_path.title: The Transfer Path
gs_transfer_path.beats:
A weekday at U.A. Academy, the week after villains attacked Class 1-A at the USJ. In the General Studies Classrooms, Class 1-C's homeroom teacher spends first period on the Sports Festival, now less than two weeks away, and on the rule in every student handbook: a General Studies student with a strong showing there can be considered for a transfer into the Hero Course, and a Hero Course student who falls short can be moved out. Most of the room sat the Hero Course entrance exam and missed. Nobody says so. At the back, Hitoshi Shinso listens with his chin on one hand, asks nothing, and is still in his seat when the room empties for lunch.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: the argument starts before the teacher is out the door and follows the class to Lunch Rush's Cafeteria. One side says the Hero Course looks straight through General Studies and the country only hears about Class 1-A. The other calls the festival rigged for flashy Quirks and wants nobody embarrassing themselves. A few plan to go and look at Class 1-A for themselves after the last bell. Shinso eats alone by the window and answers any question about his plans with a question back.

In the classroom, the party can catch Shinso before he leaves and get a few dry words out of him, never what his Quirk does; he turns sympathy aside and respects a straight question. In the cafeteria, the party can take a side, cool the argument, or ask each classmate what they would actually do in the Hero Course. A party that says aloud it means to try for the transfer is laughed at by some and quietly asked for help by others.

By canon default, Shinso joins the crowd at Class 1-A's door after classes and tells them, level and unhurried, that General Studies is coming for their places; the party may walk with him, try to stop him or hear about it that evening.

The event is complete when the last bell rings and the party has decided, aloud or privately, whether it is aiming for the transfer.

gs_shinso_training.title: Shinso's Night Training
gs_shinso_training.beats:
An evening in late spring at U.A. Academy, some weeks after the Sports Festival. The Athletics Field should be empty once the clubs leave; tonight the floodlights at one end are on. Shota Aizawa stands on the turf with a spare capture scarf over one arm, and Hitoshi Shinso, in a gym uniform already torn at one knee, is trying to throw the other end around a practice post and keeps wrapping himself instead. Nobody announced this. Aizawa watched Shinso at the festival and saw a Quirk that can end a fight in one word and a body never trained to finish one, and he offered the hours after class. The training promises nothing.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Aizawa runs drills in short, flat sentences: footwork, breakfalls, the weight of the scarf, reading a target's breathing before the throw. Shinso misses the same catch for an hour and does not ask to stop. If it rains or the night turns cold, they move into the Main Gymnasium, where the high roof gives the scarf room and the mats spare his elbows. Aizawa's only comment is "Again."

A General Studies party that stumbles on this decides what to do with what it saw. It can watch from the low concrete stand and keep the secret, spot Shinso on his falls, or ask to join. Aizawa answers fairly: this is not a club, he has no hours to teach all of 1-C, and anyone who wants more must first show they will come back tomorrow; he can hand out a few drills to practice alone and nothing more. Shinso dislikes an audience and hates pity, but he will take a partner who never mentions it in class. Asked why he keeps at it, he answers with a question, and maybe, late, with half an honest answer about being taken seriously.

Whether any of this leads to a transfer is not decided tonight, and not by anyone here.

The event is complete when Aizawa calls the session, cuts the floodlights and sends both students back to the dorms before curfew.

gs_careers_day.title: Careers Day
gs_careers_day.beats:
A weekday in mid-August, a couple of weeks after Kamino. Under the new lockdown rules any trip off campus needs a teacher's signature and a fixed return time, so the General Studies careers outing to Musutafu Police Headquarters runs on a strict clock: one bus from U.A. Academy's Campus Bus Terminal, back before evening roll call. At the Front Desk, Sansa Tamakawa walks the class past the ticket machine, the wanted posters and the walk-in line; upstairs, under escort, Naomasa Tsukauchi gives the group twenty minutes in the Detectives' Office. A fire captain and a rescue paramedic from the city services came along to speak as well.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: the speakers show the hero world from the side the cameras skip. Police hold the cordons, take the statements and file the reports after every rescue; firefighters go where no Quirk helps; paramedics carry out the people heroes find. Nobody pretends Kamino went well. Officers from across the region worked that night evacuating blocks that were no longer standing, All Might has retired, the top of the rankings feels empty, petty crime has climbed ever since, and every service is short of people. Tsukauchi separates what is public from what he cannot discuss and says plainly when he is declining to answer.

A General Studies party can ask the hard questions, ask how someone with an ordinary Quirk gets into this work, or catch Tsukauchi alone for a minute; a lie to him earns a short pause and a polite next question. A student still set on the Hero Course hears what heroes owe the people who stand beside them. One who has let that go hears about careers where the Quirk barely matters and the work matters a great deal.

If the scene starts at U.A. Academy, it opens on the sign-out sheet, the bus and a classmate who nearly did not get permission to come.

The event is complete when the class is back on the bus with a careers form each and the party has decided what to write on it.

gs_festival_booth.title: The Cultural Festival Booth
gs_festival_booth.beats:
The last week before the U.A. School Festival. After classes the General Studies Classrooms at U.A. Academy are full of cardboard, paint and argument: Class 1-C has a booth to build and no agreement on what it is. Security frames everything. Guests will be screened at the Main Gate, the barrier stays up, and the teachers have said it plainly: one alarm ends the day for everyone. The rules arrive in a stack: no open flames, no smoke machines, no sirens or flashing lights that could be mistaken for an alert, every electrical item checked by the Development Studio, every decoration approved.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: half the class wants a haunted house, half wants a cafe, and a loud few want a quiz show on pro heroes' Quirks. The Courtyard has the best foot traffic, and 1-C's stretch of it is double-booked: Mina Ashido has been drilling Class 1-A's dancers through the same eight counts on that paving every afternoon, and the band's rehearsals carry across campus. Some of 1-C grumble that the Hero Course caused the security and now takes the spotlight too; others admit the show sounds good. Hitoshi Shinso agrees to whatever is decided, does his share of cutting and painting, and leaves early every evening without saying where he goes.

Under the cardboard sits the real question: what kind of class 1-C wants guests to see when most of them come for the Hero Course. Extras, rivals, or something that stands on its own.

In the classroom, the party can broker a booth everyone will actually work on, take charge of the build, or carry the rules fight to the faculty. In the Courtyard, it can negotiate with Ashido for the space, which she trades cheerfully for help with the dance's props, or pick a fight that feeds the grumbling. The festival itself, and what happens on its day, is not part of this scene.

The event is complete when the booth is chosen, the space is settled and the first wall of it is standing.

gs_transfer_trial_eve.title: The Transfer Trial Eve
gs_transfer_trial_eve.beats:
Evenings in the last days before the Joint Training. Word has reached the General Studies Classrooms at U.A. Academy: when Classes 1-A and 1-B meet at Training Ground Gamma, Hitoshi Shinso will fight a round on each side, with the teachers watching, as his transfer trial. Nobody told 1-C officially. Shinso has not confirmed it, which the class takes as confirmation.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: after the last class the room talks about little else. Some are proud and say so loudly once he is out of earshot; some are sour that the one classmate who got this far may leave the rest behind; one asks whether anyone will notice the empty desk, and nobody answers. On the Athletics Field after dark, Shinso trains under a single floodlight with the capture scarf he has worked at since spring: throws at the posts, falls, gets up, and rehearses lines meant for opponents who already know to stay silent. Shota Aizawa looks in once, says that rest is part of training, and leaves him to it.

Shinso accepts help on his own terms. He will take a partner who throws real attacks, times his drills or plays a Hero Course opponent who refuses to answer him, and he turns away pity and pep talks alike. Asked what happens to Class 1-C if he goes, he is quiet for a long moment, then says dryly that they will manage.

In the classroom, the party can steer the class toward a send-off, a card, a shared lunch or a plain good luck, or let the sourness stand. On the field, it can push him through one more round or tell him to sleep.

The trial's outcome belongs to the Joint Training itself; nothing in this scene settles it.

The event is complete when Shinso calls it a night, or the class settles how it will see him off.

sup_hatsume_babies.title: Hatsume's Babies
sup_hatsume_babies.beats:
The Support Course's first full week of real workshop time at U.A. Academy. Mornings run in the Support Course Classrooms, lectures on materials and drafting over the hum of the 3D printers; in the afternoons everyone files through the connecting door into Power Loader's Development Studio. Mei Hatsume of Class 1-H has been there since before homeroom.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Hatsume's babies fail in ways the course will talk about all year. A pair of hover soles lifts her half a meter and pitches her into the parts shelf. A grapple launcher fires the grapple, the cable and most of the launcher. A wrist-mounted power pack runs hot, smokes and goes off with a bang that rattles the test cage, and Power Loader is shouting "Hatsume!" before the smoke clears. He hits the shutoff, clears the room, digs through the debris with his claws to fish out the pieces, and lectures the whole class on goggles, fire blankets and why every power supply needs a cutoff. Hatsume takes notes on the failure, beaming, and starts version two.

A Support Course party lives in the blast radius. In the studio, it can borrow her lathe, get drafted as a test pilot, spot the flaw in the power pack before it blows, or keep its own project from becoming collateral damage. In the classroom, it can get ahead on the design theory everyone else is skimming, or sketch an idea its classmates laugh at until it works. Power Loader respects a student who can explain why a part failed, and takes tools away from anyone who skips the checklist twice. The other first-years of 1-F to 1-H are ordinary, nervous and competitive, and most have already learned to stand well back from Hatsume's bench.

The event is complete when the studio is swept, the party's first project has been tested once, and Power Loader signs the day's safety log.

sup_showcase_prep.title: Festival Showcase Prep
sup_showcase_prep.beats:
The last days before the Sports Festival, afternoons in the Development Studio at U.A. Academy. For the Hero Course the festival is a stage for agency scouts; for the Support Course it is a showroom. Support companies send scouts to the stands, the festival rules let Support students compete with gear they built themselves, and every second on the national broadcast is free advertising. Power Loader has posted a sign-off sheet: anything going into the stadium is tested here first, in the cage, with him watching.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Mei Hatsume has a plan for every event and a baby for every plan, and she lays it out for anyone in range: hover soles for a race, a jet pack for whatever comes next, a grappling arm, a sensor visor, each tagged with the company she wants to notice it. Winning matters to her only as a way to be seen winning with her gear. She tries to recruit the party as a teammate, a test pilot or a walking display stand. Power Loader sends half her list back for missing cutoffs and unshielded batteries, then signs the rest with a sigh, because it is good work.

A Support Course party decides what to bring and why. It can build one thing that works every time, chase a showpiece that might fail on live television, or design something for a Hero Course student who asked for help, though the rules on Hero Course students using others' gear are strict and Power Loader makes the party read them twice. It can fight Hatsume for the cage's test slots, team up with her, or keep its own design secret until the day. A failure in the cage is cheap; a failure in the stadium is national.

Nothing about the festival's events or results is decided in this scene.

The event is complete when the party's festival gear passes Power Loader's sign-off, or the party decides to go in without any.

sup_costume_rush.title: Costume Upgrade Rush
sup_costume_rush.beats:
Late summer at U.A. Academy, the weeks before the Provisional License Exam. Class 1-A is developing special moves all day, and every new move breaks something: a glove, a boot, a seam, a sensor. The Hero Course arrives at the Development Studio in a steady line, change-request forms in hand, and Power Loader vanishes behind a stack of paperwork that grows faster than he can sign it.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Mei Hatsume is delighted. Every request is a chance to build, and every visitor is a customer and a test pilot at once. Izuku Midoriya comes in with Tenya Iida and Ochaco Uraraka to ask about protecting his arms and putting more power into his kicks; by canon default the studio fits him with forearm guards and iron soles for his boots. One of Hatsume's other babies goes off as they arrive, the door blows open and she lands on Izuku in the smoke, reciting specs before she stands up; Iida lectures on safety, Uraraka cannot stop laughing, and Power Loader sighs and fishes the parts out of the hallway. Behind them the requests stack up: fabric that will not tear in a fall, a sensor that warns of overheating, a strap that holds under a weight-changing Quirk.

A Support Course party gets a real client: one request off the pile, from a Hero Course student who needs it before the exam. It can take measurements, ask how the student's Quirk actually moves, which is always Power Loader's first question, and build something that holds up on exam day. It can help Hatsume with the iron soles, stop her from turning a simple brace into a rocket, or help Power Loader clear the forms, which earns his trust faster than any invention.

The event is complete when the party's commission passes its first test in the cage and the client signs for it.

sup_support_expo.title: The Support Expo
sup_support_expo.beats:
A weekend in early autumn. One of the mid-sized houses on Theater Row in Central Tokyo has been rented for a support-item trade show: booths from the big support companies and a dozen small ones crowd the lobby and aisles, the stage runs live demonstrations, recruiters hand out cards, and several schools with support programs have student tables. U.A. Academy's Support Course has signed out a small group under Power Loader's supervision, by bus from the Campus Bus Terminal and back before evening roll call, as the lockdown rules require.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Mei Hatsume came to sell, not to look. She has her babies laid out before the doors open, stops every company scout who slows down, and demonstrates a jet pack indoors until an usher objects. At the next table a prodigy from a rival school draws a crowd with a small, quiet device that works every single time, and the two start a contest neither will admit to. Mid-afternoon an independent inventor's pitch goes wrong on the main stage: a powered rig jams, overheats and starts to smoke in front of a full house. Power Loader is already moving toward it, and someone at the U.A. table is closer.

A Support Course party chooses what it came for. It can pitch its own work, study what the industry builds for working heroes, help Hatsume win the room or keep her from scaring off a sponsor, and befriend or outdo the rival prodigy. On stage, it can help bring the rig down safely and spare the inventor some dignity, or watch Hatsume turn the rescue into a sales pitch. A company card or an invitation to send designs is a real result; a signed contract is not, not this year.

If the scene starts at U.A. Academy, it opens at dawn with crates going onto the bus and Hatsume arguing about how many more will fit.

The event is complete when the expo closes, the U.A. group is back on the bus and the party has counted what it brought home.

sup_workshop_overnight.title: Workshop Overnight
sup_workshop_overnight.beats:
A winter night at U.A. Academy, well past the hour the Development Studio should be dark. A Hero Course student's gear failed in training this afternoon: the mount of a grapple line cracked under load, and the student is due on the field for morning drills with it or without it. The repair request came to the Support Course stamped urgent. Mei Hatsume claimed the job first, as she claims everything, and already has the whole assembly in pieces on her bench.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Power Loader is meant to send everyone back to the dorms by curfew. Tonight he signs late passes, starts the coffee maker and stays, which he will deny tomorrow. The night runs on solder, canned coffee and Hatsume talking to the parts. Around midnight she decides the original mount was the wrong idea and starts a redesign that would be better and slower; Power Loader wants the simple fix, tested twice, done by dawn. The argument is technical, fast and not unfriendly. Around three in the morning the first rebuilt mount cracks in the test cage.

A Support Course party is the third pair of hands. It can take the safe fix and get it exactly right, back Hatsume's redesign and race the clock, find out why the first mount cracked, or be the one who makes everyone stop and eat something. Power Loader tests the final piece himself before it leaves the studio, and he will not pass anything that might fail on someone's arm. A student who stays the night learns more about how he thinks than any lecture teaches.

The event is complete when the repaired gear passes its test in the cage and is boxed for the morning, or Power Loader calls it off and sends everyone to bed.

man_pr_101.title: Hero PR 101
man_pr_101.beats:
April at U.A. Academy, a weekday lesson in the Management Course Classrooms: the first lecture of Hero Business Fundamentals. The lecturer, a former press director for a top-ten agency, writes three words on the board: ranking, sponsor, image. The Hero Billboard Chart weighs incidents resolved, contribution to society and public approval; sponsors pay for a logo on a costume, a patrol route or a face on a drink can; and every agency, the lecturer says, sells the same product under different labels: the feeling of being safe.

Then the case study. Class 1-A has been in the news twice this month: reporters stormed the grounds when the U.A. Barrier crumbled at the Main Gate, and days later the League of Villains attacked the class at the USJ until All Might arrived. Headlines and comment threads go up on the screen. The default course, as pressure the player can change: the class splits. One side calls 1-A a brand at risk, a class attacked twice in a month that sponsors will read as danger; the other calls it the most valuable first-year class in the country, the students who survived villains with All Might as their teacher. The lecturer lets the argument run, then asks each student to pick one Hero Course first-year and write the single sentence an agency would print on a poster about them.

Midway through, Nemuri Kayama steps in as a guest for twenty minutes on the costume that made the hero world write new rules, and on why a hero's image belongs to the hero first and the agency second; she enjoys the question about scandal far too much. The Sports Festival is less than two weeks away and the Management Course competes in it too, so the homework is to watch it as a market, not a contest, and note which faces the cameras love. A player who argues well can win the room, earn Nemuri Kayama's attention or find a partner for the semester's brand project.

The event is complete when the lecture ends and the player's poster sentence is written, read aloud or refused.

man_offer_board.title: The Offer Board
man_offer_board.beats:
One of the two days off after the U.A. Sports Festival, at U.A. Academy. Most of the campus sleeps in, but the Management Course Classrooms are open: the agencies' internship offers for the Hero Course are pouring in by mail, fax and courier, and the faculty has handed the count to the Management Course as a live case study, due before Friday's Hero Name Day. Shota Aizawa sets two crates of envelopes on a desk, says the tally should be correct and short, and leaves for a nap. Vlad King stays, arms folded, watching the Class 1-B column.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: the tally follows the Festival as it was actually played. By canon default Shoto Todoroki leads with 4,123 offers and Katsuki Bakugo, the champion who had to be chained to the podium, has 3,556; then Fumikage Tokoyami 360, Tenya Iida 301 although he left the stadium early for his brother, Denki Kaminari 272, Momo Yaoyorozu 108, Eijiro Kirishima 68, Ochaco Uraraka 20 and Hanta Sero 14. Izuku Midoriya, who won the obstacle race and broke himself against Todoroki, has none. Class 1-B's column is thin, and Vlad King blames a month of headlines about 1-A, loudly. The celebrity hero Uwabami's agency has sent offers to Momo Yaoyorozu and Itsuka Kendo with a line about commercial work.

The lecturer wants analysis, not a list: which agencies chased fame and which chased a skill, which offer is really an advertising contract, and why a famous father's name outweighs a broken arm. The class fights over method, a stack of late envelopes turns up under a desk, and one agency's letter asks bluntly about Bakugo's temper. A sharp player can write a case Aizawa actually reads to the end, or one Vlad King carries straight to Principal Nezu.

The event is complete when the tally and the analysis are handed in for Hero Name Day, or the party leaves the classroom.

man_crisis_pr.title: Crisis PR After Kamino
man_crisis_pr.beats:
The week after Kamino, at U.A. Academy. The country watched All Might's last fight live, saw his body give way to a thin, wounded man on camera, and has now heard him retire from hero work. U.A. is where the questions land: the League of Villains took a student from a U.A. training camp, U.A.'s apology to the press afterward went badly, and the campus is locking down behind new walls, sensors and a stricter curfew. Reporters crowd the Main Gate again, parents' emails fill the office, and two of the academy's sponsors have asked for a call.

In the Management Course Classrooms the hero business lecturer scraps the syllabus. The class gets real material, cleared by the principal: the press questions, a stack of anonymized parent complaints, the sponsors' notes. The default course, as pressure the player can change: the class drafts responses in teams and splits between honesty and reassurance. One team wants U.A. to apologize again; another wants to sell the lockdown as safety; a third wants All Might's face nowhere near any of it.

At the Main Gate, Present Mic stands between the reporters and the grounds, quieter than anyone has heard him, answering nothing. A team sent to observe sees one careless quote turn into an evening headline, and a reporter tries to get a Management student to say something about the Hero Course on camera.

The best draft goes up to Principal Nezu in the Principal's Office. He offers tea, reads it twice, asks one question that takes it apart and one that puts it back together, and may use a line of it at the next briefing.

Public facts only: what aired from Kamino, the retirement, the camp raid, the lockdown. Nobody on this campus explains why All Might's power gave out, and the narration does not guess.

The event is complete when the class's response is delivered to Nezu or to the press at the gate, or the party leaves the scene.

man_agency_placement.title: Agency Office Placement
man_agency_placement.beats:
September, in the weeks after the provisional license exam. The Management Course sends its first-years out for a week on the business side of a working hero agency, and the scene meets the party wherever it is: a placement letter, a train ride, a front desk with three phones. The agency is a mid-size office in Musutafu or near the party; its head is a working pro too busy to look up, and its staff are an office manager who actually runs everything, a tired publicist and a dispatcher in a headset. All of them are generic people; no canon hero runs this office.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: since All Might retired, call volume has doubled and the patrol schedule no longer fits the sidekicks the agency can pay. The office manager hands the student the week. Rebuild the patrol rota so nobody works three nights in a row. Sit in on the quarterly call with a sponsor, a regional bakery chain that wants its logo on camera and is nervous about a property damage claim from last month. Answer the public line, where a lost cat, a noise complaint and a frightened caller who saw someone climbing a roof all count. Draft the agency's two-line comment for a reporter asking whether small agencies can hold the line now that the Symbol of Peace is gone. Endeavor's name comes up in every meeting, and the newly licensed students from U.A. and Shiketsu are everyone's recruiting topic.

Midweek, dispatch sends the pro out during the sponsor call and leaves the student holding it alone; the sponsor stays or walks on what the student says. A rota that ignores the sidekicks' rest gets one of them hurt on a late patrol by Friday, minor and preventable; a fair rota holds. The publicist steals the best line from the student's draft and takes the credit unless someone objects.

The event is complete when the week's rota is posted, the sponsor's decision is in and the office manager signs the student's placement report.

man_festival_marketing.title: Festival Marketing
man_festival_marketing.beats:
The last days before the U.A. School Festival, at U.A. Academy. Principal Nezu has won permission to hold it at all, on strict terms: invitation-only guests screened at the Main Gate, police on the perimeter, and a single alarm cancels the day. The Management Course has the job of selling a festival nobody can simply walk into: the invitation list, sponsor booths in the Courtyard, a printed program, the posters, and a reason for the public to think of U.A. as a school again after Kamino.

In the Management Course Classrooms, the default course as pressure the player can change: the lecturer gives the class two days and a budget too small for its ambitions. Teams fight over what to lead with: the Hero Course stage show, the Support Course's exhibits, or the cafes and stalls of the other courses, which still blame the Hero Course for the lockdown. A sponsor wants its logo above the stage; the invitation list has room for families and a few local businesses, and none for the press.

In the Courtyard the poster war breaks out. Kyoka Jiro, who leads Class 1-A's band, wants the poster plain: date, time, stage. Mina Ashido, who runs the dance, wants lights, glitter and every face in the class. Neito Monoma arrives with a draft for Class 1-B's play twice the size, insists the program list it first, then asks whether the Management Course takes commissions to keep Class 1-A off the cover. Whatever the class picks, somebody storms off, and the player can broker one poster everybody can live with, sell two, or let the Hero Course fight it out while the deadline passes.

The event is complete when the festival's promotion plan is approved and the posters go up, or the party leaves before the fight is settled.

fac_staff_meeting.title: The First Staff Meeting
fac_staff_meeting.beats:
Evening in the Teachers' Lounge at U.A. Academy, the first week of classes. Principal Nezu pours tea for everyone before the first agenda item, which the veterans know is a bad sign. Around the table: Shota Aizawa half inside his sleeping bag, Present Mic narrating the agenda, Nemuri Kayama with her boots on a spare chair, Cementoss, Ectoplasm, Hound Dog, Power Loader smelling of smoke, Recovery Girl with a bag of gummies, Thirteen over from the USJ, Vlad King, and the newest hire, All Might, too big for his chair and reading from a card headed How to Teach.

The agenda, by default: reporters have camped at the Main Gate all week asking for All Might; Thirteen books Class 1-A's first rescue lesson at the USJ with Aizawa and All Might; the Sports Festival committee needs volunteers. Then the real fight. Aizawa ran his Quirk Apprehension Test on the first day and told Class 1-A that last place would be expelled; he expelled an entire class last year. Vlad King calls it cruel at full volume. Nemuri Kayama teases Aizawa for calling it a logical ruse afterward. Recovery Girl notes that she spent the afternoon mending a first-year's finger. All Might, nervous, asks whether failing a student is ever a kindness and gets a flat look.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: Nezu defends the free hand he gives every teacher and lets the room decide nothing. A new teacher at the table is introduced, receives a course load and one of the chores (the press at the gate, the festival committee, a club advisorship) and is asked to take a side on expulsions. A veteran can shift the debate with a story or a vote; Nezu enjoys any argument that surprises him, and Present Mic narrates every point scored.

The event is complete when Nezu closes the meeting and hands out the week's assignments, or the party leaves the lounge.

fac_grading_night.title: Grading Night
fac_grading_night.beats:
Night in the Teachers' Lounge at U.A. Academy, in the days after the final exams. Score sheets, monitor footage and cold coffee cover every table, beside a tray from Lunch Rush that nobody has touched. The faculty grades the practical pair by pair before results go out.

By canon default, unless the exams went otherwise: Eijiro Kirishima and Rikido Sato failed against Cementoss, who says calmly that they never once tried to go around his walls; Denki Kaminari and Mina Ashido failed against Principal Nezu, who is still pleased with how Training Ground Gamma came down; Hanta Sero slept through Nemuri Kayama's aroma while Minoru Mineta passed. Vlad King reports that Class 1-B passed except for Neito Monoma, and takes it personally. The loudest argument is All Might's match against Izuku Midoriya and Katsuki Bakugo: Recovery Girl wants to know why one student came through the gate unconscious, Snipe and Ectoplasm call it the closest thing to a real fight in the whole exam, and All Might, rubbing his neck, insists the two earned the pass together.

Then Aizawa says what he planned all along: everyone goes to the summer camp, failures included, with extra lessons at night. He calls the threat of staying behind a logical ruse. Vlad King objects that it rewards failure; Present Mic laughs until he coughs; Cementoss asks only that the extra lessons be real; Thirteen and Power Loader want their own pairs' marks read into the record first.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: the grades are argued and signed tonight. A faculty party graded a pair of its own and must defend the mark, can push a borderline pass or fail, and can side with Aizawa's ruse or against it. Nezu has the last word and the last cup of tea.

The event is complete when every practical grade is signed and the camp roster is set, or the party leaves the lounge.

fac_night_rounds.title: Night Rounds
fac_night_rounds.beats:
Late at night at Heights Alliance, U.A. Academy, in the weeks after Kamino. Since the lockdown began, the faculty walks the dorms every night in pairs: the Heights Alliance Yard, the doors, then each lounge. Tonight's round pairs the party with Hound Dog, who reads the yard by scent, while Vlad King takes Class 1-B's side and can be heard from the yard.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: Hound Dog's nose finds the first curfew breaker within a minute. Eijiro Kirishima is out in the yard in a T-shirt, hardening his arms and punching the dark because he cannot sleep, and he apologizes with a full bow before anyone asks. In the Class 1-A Dorm Lounge the television is on low; Toru Hagakure, a floating pair of pajamas and a blanket, says she is only counting heads, and her voice is too bright. Katsuki Bakugo comes down for water, sees a teacher, says nothing and does not go back up. In the Class 1-B Dorm Lounge, Itsuka Kendo is still up with a cup of tea, making sure nobody in her class is awake alone, which means she is.

Somebody wants to talk, and which one depends on how the party carries itself. A teacher who hands out curfew slips gets compliance and silence; one who sits down gets a question with no good answer: about the camp, about Kamino, about whether the new walls will hold. Hound Dog growls at every broken rule and then, when a student finally talks, stays to listen. Nobody is in danger tonight; the stake is whether a student goes to bed lighter than they came down.

A teacher answers from what is public and from what that teacher has seen; staff secrets stay secret.

The event is complete when the round is finished and every student is back in their room, or the party ends the round early.

fac_license_plans.title: License Exam Lesson Plans
fac_license_plans.beats:
Late summer at U.A. Academy, the weeks before the provisional license exam. Shota Aizawa has told the Hero Course to build at least two Ultimate Moves, signature techniques built on each student's Quirk, before the exam, and the faculty has turned the Main Gymnasium into a training hall. Cementoss raises cliffs, pillars and broken stairs out of the floor on request; Ectoplasm fills them with clones, one per student, and lets each fight until a move works or fails. All Might, retired and thin in a loose suit, watches from the side with a notebook and gives plain advice.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: by midmorning Izuku Midoriya has stopped punching and started kicking, sparing his scarred arms, and All Might cannot stop smiling; Katsuki Bakugo is blowing clones apart with a tighter, narrower blast; a dozen others are stuck. At lunch in the Teachers' Lounge the plan becomes an argument. Aizawa wants the slowest students pushed hardest. Cementoss reports that the floor needs more repairs than he can make by tomorrow and that two students trained through injuries. Vlad King wants equal gym hours for Class 1-B, which sits the exam at a different venue, and says so. Power Loader has a stack of costume change requests and no time. Ectoplasm names, in two sentences, who is not ready.

A teacher party sets the rota, runs a session, rules on who gets the gym, or benches a student who is not ready for a day. Pushing a tired student too hard costs a sprain and a lecture from Recovery Girl; holding back too much costs a move nobody finishes before the exam.

The event is complete when the day's sessions end and next week's training plan is agreed, or the party leaves.

fac_staff_party.title: Year-End Staff Party
fac_staff_party.beats:
Late December, evening, in the Teachers' Lounge at U.A. Academy. The desks are pushed to the walls; Nemuri Kayama has hung lights and set the dress code, and Present Mic has wired his speaker collar to a playlist and appointed himself host. Lunch Rush's trays cover one table; Power Loader has built a hot pot burner that has not caught fire yet. For once everyone is out of costume, in party clothes: Principal Nezu with a speech on cards, Shota Aizawa near the door, All Might in a suit that finally fits his new frame, Cementoss, Ectoplasm, Snipe, Hound Dog, Recovery Girl, Thirteen and Vlad King.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: Nezu's toast runs long and wanders into the state of his fur, then lands on the year: the USJ, the camp, Kamino, All Might's retirement, a festival held behind walls, the first chart without All Might at the top, and a whole first year that made it to December. Nemuri Kayama runs a party game of questions that Hound Dog refuses and Snipe wins without saying a word. Present Mic gets the room singing. Vlad King and Aizawa argue the Joint Training result again. All Might tells a story at his own expense and the room laughs with him, not at him. Aizawa tries to leave three times, and Mic and Nemuri Kayama catch him twice. If the raid freed Eri, he has a better excuse than anyone: she is asleep in the teachers' quarters and he wants to be there if she wakes.

Late in the evening someone goes quiet over what the year cost, and the party can sit with them or let the music cover it. A teacher party can give a toast of its own, start a rivalry over the karaoke list or help Aizawa escape. Between colleagues, romance stays at most a hint.

The event is complete when Nezu's last toast is drunk and the lounge empties, or Aizawa finally gets out the door with the party's help.

civ_moving_day.title: Moving Day
civ_moving_day.beats:
The first days of April and of the new fiscal year, a weekday from morning into evening. Cherry trees bloom, new hires in stiff suits pack the trains, and reporters still camp at U.A. Academy's gate for a glimpse of All Might. Today the player moves into a new apartment in their own city, a short ride from work, wherever the Background puts home. If the Background has the player settled for years, the move belongs to a new neighbor across the hall who has buried the corridor in boxes, and the player is the helper.

Who is there: the landlord, Mrs. Setsuko Haraguchi, a brisk retired bookkeeper on the ground floor who carries the garbage calendar in a plastic sleeve; two tired movers; the upstairs neighbor, Daichi Ono, a night-shift nurse whose Quirk lets him hear a dropped coin through two floors and who wants quiet above all; down the hall, Mrs. Kinue Abe, whose mild magnetic Quirk keeps teaspoons stuck to her palm, bringing tea unasked. Mr. Tatsuya Moriwaki runs the corner store at the end of the block and knows every resident's complaints.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: the truck arrives an hour early while the keys are still with Mrs. Haraguchi, the stairs are the only way up, and the box with the kettle and the bedding went onto the wrong truck. The landlord walks through burnable, non-burnable and bottle days and mentions that the last tenant left over noise. At noon Daichi comes down, sleepless, about the stairs. Neighbors expect a small greeting gift, and Moriwaki sells boxed towels and soba for exactly that. A Quirk inside the building is a private matter; one used on the street out front can still bring a fine. In Tokyo the room is smaller, the rent higher and the landlord a management company on the phone.

The event is complete when the last box is inside, the missing box is found or written off, and the player has met the landlord and at least one neighbor, or leaves the unpacking for another day.

civ_festival_fever.title: Festival Fever
civ_festival_fever.beats:
Golden Week, the days after the U.A. Sports Festival. The scene reaches the player wherever the day goes. Replays loop on station boards, shop televisions and phones. By canon default, unless the story changed it, the whole country watched Katsuki Bakugo win the first-year tournament and rage on the podium in chains and a muzzle because Shoto Todoroki held back his fire in the final; Izuku Midoriya win the obstacle race and wreck his own fingers against Todoroki; Ochaco Uraraka refuse to quit against Bakugo; Fumikage Tokoyami take third, and Tenya Iida, also third, leave before the ceremony when word came that his brother Ingenium had been attacked in Hosu by the Hero Killer.

Who is there: at work, Kenji Watabe, a coworker who has rewatched the final eleven times and calls that podium honest; the manager, Ms. Yumiko Hosaka, who wants the screen off because people stop to watch and block the aisle; Mr. Shiraishi, a retired regular, who says a hero who snarls on a podium should never be licensed.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: Kenji and Mr. Shiraishi start a loud argument over the podium, a line forms behind them, and Ms. Hosaka asks the player to end it. Later a first-year in a U.A. tracksuit, a Support Course student seen for half a minute in the obstacle race, comes in for a drink; three customers recognize her at once, one wants a photo, and she only wants out. If the player sat in the stands on festival day, a regular swears the player was in a crowd shot behind the food stalls.

At a cafe the replay plays on one phone at a table of six; at a ramen shop it runs above the counter between orders; on a delivery route every door asks about the final; near Tokyo's scramble crossing the giant screens loop the podium while the crowd stalls on the crosswalk.

The event is complete when the argument at work is settled or broken up and the recognized student has her drink and leaves, with or without a photo, or the player's shift ends.

civ_after_kamino.title: After Kamino
civ_after_kamino.beats:
Mid-August, the days after Kamino. Every screen still carries the footage: a block of Kamino Ward flattened, All Might's body giving out on live television, a thin, wounded man in the rubble, then one last blow and a finger pointed at the camera. Unless the story changed it, the kidnapped U.A. student Katsuki Bakugo is home, Best Jeanist is recovering from his injuries, the masked man the news calls Shigaraki's Sensei is in custody, and All Might has retired from hero work. Endeavor is now the highest-ranked active hero, and talk shows argue whether he can stand for anything. Obon has begun and the trains are packed.

Who is there: the manager has set a Kamino relief box by the register; a coworker, Saki Nomura, has not slept since the broadcast and talks about moving home to the countryside; a neighbor has set All Might figures and incense on her balcony; at the station, Hiroshi Tanigawa, a volunteer coordinator in an armband, signs people up for a morning bus to Kamino to sweep, sort salvage and hand out water behind police tape; licensed crews do the heavy lifting.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: the day runs on short tempers and small fears. Customers buy water and batteries. In the afternoon a man with a speed Quirk grabs an armful of goods and bolts, and a sidekick from a small local agency catches him two blocks away, out of breath, saying the agency's calls have tripled since Kamino. A civilian who stops him with a Quirk risks a fine, unless it was self-defense. Saki asks the player to cover her shift so she can catch a train home.

In Musutafu, reporters crowd U.A. Academy's gate again, and new walls rise around the campus. In Tokyo the giant screens replay the retirement announcement while crowds stand still to watch.

The event is complete when the player has made one choice about the mood around them (to volunteer, give, comfort, cover a shift or keep their head down) and the day's shift or volunteer run ends.

civ_fan_convention.title: Hero Fan Convention
civ_fan_convention.beats:
A weekend in early autumn: the Hero Fan Expo fills the exhibition halls of the nearest big city, Musutafu's or Tokyo's, as the player's life sets it. The player comes as a fan, on a friend's spare ticket, or behind a booth the workplace rented.

Who is there: convention staff in orange vests under a floor manager with a headset, Ms. Haruna Ando; Tidewater, a sidekick from a mid-sized agency, signing photos at a folding table, joking about her short line; Doorstop, the stocky pro the expo hired for security, whose Quirk pins whatever he touches to the floor. All Might goods are everywhere and different now: a Symbol of Peace retirement line sells out in an hour, fans tie denim armbands for Best Jeanist's recovery, and cosplayers in Sports Festival tracksuits pose as Bakugo and Todoroki.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: the main-stage panel, Who Is Number One Now, argues the first Hero Billboard Chart without All Might, due before winter. Endeavor is the highest-ranked active hero and the room's least loved; Hawks is fast and popular; a panelist insists Best Jeanist would hold the top if he were healthy. The open mic waits for a question. Midafternoon a man in a cheap All Might costume sweeps a box of signed cards off a booth and runs for the exit; Doorstop pins him to the carpet in one move and calls security. The player can be the one robbed, the one who points, or the one in the runner's path; a Quirk used outside self-defense is still illegal here, and Doorstop says so politely. Tidewater's line grows for the rest of the day.

A booth worker sells out early or sits beside a stack of unsold stock; a fan chases one signature or one rare figure; a friend who bought the tickets wants a cosplay photo with the player in it.

The event is complete when the theft is handled and the player has done one thing at the expo that matters to them (a signature, a purchase, a question at the panel, a booth sold out), or leaves the hall.

civ_holiday_rush.title: Holiday Rush
civ_holiday_rush.beats:
Mid to late December, the year-end rush, afternoon into closing. The city is lit, bonus season fills the shops, Christmas cake orders stack up and year-end parties fill every izakaya. Unless the story changed it, November's Hero Billboard Chart named Endeavor Number One and Hawks Number Two, and the replay of Endeavor's fight with a flying Nomu over Fukuoka, his fist raised at the end, still runs between ads.

Who is there: the manager, Mr. Masaru Iwata, short-staffed and apologizing in advance; a part-timer, Ayumi Kuroda, saving for a trip; a stream of customers; a local hero on patrol, Snapline, whose Quirk fires a taut cord from either wrist.

The default course, as pressure the player can change: a coworker calls in sick and Mr. Iwata asks the player to stay two extra hours. The cake preorders are mixed up and two customers claim the same box. Near dusk a man with a Quirk that fogs glass clouds the front window and the register camera, grabs a stack of gift cards and the cash tray, and runs; Snapline, passing outside, has him wrapped on the sidewalk in seconds, poses for one phone, and leaves the statements to a police officer. Any civilian who uses a Quirk on the thief risks a fine, unless it was self-defense. The rush resumes.

At a convenience store it is cakes and fried chicken; at a cafe, seasonal drinks and couples at every table; at a ramen shop, party groups ordering one more round; on a delivery route, three times the packages and dark stairwells; at a shop counter, gift wrapping until the tape runs out. Near Tokyo's scramble crossing the stores overflow under the giant screens.

After closing the shutters come down and the noise stops. Mr. Iwata hands out leftover cake and thanks everyone in turn; Ayumi buys hot canned coffee from the vending machine and asks what the player plans for the New Year.

The event is complete when the shop closes for the night after the robbery is handled and the player has shared the quiet after closing or gone home.

b1_day_after_usj.title: The Day After the USJ
b1_day_after_usj.beats:
The day after the attack on the USJ, at U.A. Academy. Classes are called off across campus while the faculty meet, and the Class 1-B Dorm Lounge fills early. Every channel runs the same aerial shot of the dome and the police tape across the road, and the anchors repeat what the school has confirmed: a group calling itself the League of Villains broke into Class 1-A's rescue lesson, two teachers are hurt, All Might drove the attackers off, police hold dozens of thugs, and the ringleaders got away. No student died. The Class 1-A side of the building is very quiet.

Itsuka Kendo has made tea for anyone who wants it and makes sure every worried family on the phone gets an answer. Tetsutetsu Tetsutetsu paces and wants to go next door and do something. Ibara Shiozaki prays for the injured. Pony Tsunotori asks what "villain alliance" means in the anchor's fast Japanese, and Setsuna Tokage explains it at speed.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Neito Monoma watches with folded arms and announces that 1-A is now famous for being attacked, that the cameras will follow them all the way to the Sports Festival, and that 1-B will have to be twice as good to be seen at all. The room goes cold. Kendo chops him in the back of the neck before he finishes and apologizes to the room for him. Then Vlad King walks in from the faculty meeting, turns off the screen and says it plainly: the timetable could have put 1-B in that dome. Training gets harder from tomorrow, and anyone who wants to help 1-A can start by being ready.

The party can steady a shaken classmate, push back on Monoma or find the grain of sense in what he said, keep Tetsutetsu from storming next door, or ask Vlad King what the faculty knows; he shares only what the news has. If the scene opens the next morning instead, the same talk happens in the Class 1-B Homeroom before first period.

The event is complete when Vlad King has spoken and the class settles on getting ready, or the party leaves.

b1_monoma_provocation.title: Monoma's Provocation
b1_monoma_provocation.beats:
Lunchtime in the days after Hero Name Day, at Lunch Rush's Cafeteria at U.A. Academy. The internship lists are posted and the Sports Festival replays are still everywhere; strangers recognize Class 1-A on the train, and Class 1-B has noticed. Neito Monoma, newly Phantom Thief, has opened a campaign. All morning he drifted past 1-A in the Main Building Hallway with a slow clap and a question about how fame feels, and now he carries his tray to the table where Katsuki Bakugo, Eijiro Kirishima and Momo Yaoyorozu are eating.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Monoma sets the tray down without sitting, smiles wide and asks, with exquisite courtesy, whether the podium was comfortable, and whether a winner in restraints counts as a champion in 1-A. The laugh goes on too long. Kirishima tries to laugh it off; Yaoyorozu answers with cold, precise courtesy; Bakugo does not look up, then sets down his chopsticks, and his palms start to crackle. Monoma leans closer, one hand drifting toward Bakugo's sleeve. Before contact, Itsuka Kendo, 1-B's class representative, arrives behind him, chops him once in the back of the neck, catches him and tells the table, "Sorry about him." Behind her, Tetsutetsu Tetsutetsu shouts across to Kirishima that their rematch is still on, and Sen Kaibara takes Monoma's tray away with a flat remark about lunch.

By path: a 1-B party is in Monoma's audience and can feed the act, rein him in before Kendo does, or turn the taunt into a fair challenge Bakugo will respect. A 1-A party sits at the target table: the bait is plain, and taking it means a cafeteria fight the faculty will hear about, while ignoring Monoma infuriates him more than any comeback. Either class can set up Tetsutetsu and Kirishima's rematch for another day. No real fight happens here: a Quirk used indoors brings a teacher at once.

The event is complete when Monoma has been chopped or talked down and both classes go back to lunch, or the party leaves.

b1_joint_sparring.title: Joint Sparring Day
b1_joint_sparring.beats:
A weekday afternoon in late spring at U.A. Academy. Vlad King has talked Shota Aizawa into a combined sparring block in the Main Gymnasium: not a graded exercise, only pairs from Class 1-A and Class 1-B on taped squares, a whistle, and Vlad King's insistence that his class is ready. Aizawa agreed because fighting unfamiliar Quirks is rational, and his tone says nothing else about it pleases him. If the drills move outdoors, the second half runs in the Mock City Streets of Ground Beta.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: the teachers call the pairs. Tetsutetsu Tetsutetsu and Eijiro Kirishima get each other again and charge before the whistle ends, steel against hardened skin, until both are winded and grinning; the crowd wants a winner and gets none. Itsuka Kendo draws Momo Yaoyorozu, who creates a net, a staff and then a plan; Kendo reads the plan instead of the tools, and the bout turns into a slow, careful contest of who adapts first. Neito Monoma touches three people on the way to his square and narrates every copy. He asks Katsuki Bakugo for a bout, Bakugo's answer is loud, and Aizawa's eyes glow red before an explosion leaves a palm. Ibara Shiozaki prays before her match and binds her opponent with an apology.

The rules hold: a bout stops at a call or a tap, nobody strikes a downed partner, and Aizawa erases anyone who forgets. Vlad King keeps a running tally on a whiteboard he never mentioned to Aizawa.

By path: a 1-B party is paired with a 1-A student and can win, lose well or learn the other class's habits. A 1-A party gets a 1-B opponent whose Quirk it has seen only on the Sports Festival broadcast, and Monoma will try to touch it before the whistle. Either side can turn a grudge bout into respect, or into a scene the teachers end early.

The event is complete when the last pairs bow out and the two teachers compare notes, or the party leaves.

b1_movie_night.title: 1-B Movie Night
b1_movie_night.beats:
An evening in late June in the Class 1-B Dorm Lounge at U.A. Academy. Itsuka Kendo has put the snacks in order on the low table: chips by the left armrest, rice crackers by the right, one bag open at a time so nothing ends up in the sofa. The lights are down. It is Neito Monoma's turn to pick the film, and he has chosen a long American heist picture about a gentleman thief who robs a rival's museum to prove he is the better man. He has seen it four times and quotes it under his breath.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: the film runs with commentary. Pony Tsunotori explains everything the subtitles miss: the baseball joke, the roadside diner, why the detective keeps calling everyone "buddy", the Fourth of July fireworks over the finale; she is delighted to be the expert for once. Reiko Yanagi wanted a ghost story instead, and slowly lifts a cushion behind anyone who mocks her pick. Sen Kaibara names every hole in the plot, one line each. Hiryu Rin says nothing and eats steadily. Jurota Shishida politely asks people to stop talking. Yui Kodai shrinks the empty bags without a word. Then the thief's loyal partner takes the fall for him, and Tetsutetsu Tetsutetsu cries openly and loudly and is not embarrassed in the least. Monoma declares the thief obviously the hero; Kendo points out that he is the villain.

The party can choose the next film, argue the ending, help Pony with a joke that does not translate, or catch Monoma admitting why he loves the thief: the man wins with treasures that belong to other people. Vlad King looks in around ten, asks whether this is a study group, and stays for the last twenty minutes.

The event is complete when the credits roll and Kendo assigns the cleanup, or the party leaves.

b1_kendo_study.title: Kendo's Study Session
b1_kendo_study.beats:
Evenings in the week before the final exams, in the Class 1-B Dorm Lounge at U.A. Academy. Itsuka Kendo has pushed the tables together, written a schedule on the whiteboard (hero law, then math, then modern literature, ten-minute breaks strictly enforced) and assigned tutors by subject: Juzo Honenuki on math, Nirengeki Shoda on hero law, and Kojiro Bondo, quietly the best essay writer in the class, on literature. Earlier the same group held a long table in the Library until the librarian's look sent them home.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Tetsutetsu Tetsutetsu and Togaru Kamakiri need the most help and accept it the least. Tetsutetsu attacks every problem set at full volume and declares victory before checking the answer; Kamakiri glares at a word problem and dares it to make sense. Neito Monoma sits apart with a closed book, insists he does not need a study group, and corrects everyone's answers aloud from across the room. Setsuna Tokage sends a single floating piece to peek at his notes and reports that they are color-coded. Kendo has heard from an upperclassman that the practical will be robots again, the same as the entrance exam, and passes it on with a warning that it is only a rumor; the room relaxes about the practical and dreads the written test. Nobody here knows the real format.

The party can tutor or be tutored, broker a truce between Kamakiri and an equation, or draw Monoma into the group without letting him win the argument. Kendo will take the hardest student herself unless someone offers; noticing that she has not opened her own books all week, and doing something about it, is a quiet win.

The event is complete when the night's practice quiz is graded and Kendo sends everyone to bed, or the party leaves.

b1_shopping_trip.title: The 1-B Shopping Trip
b1_shopping_trip.beats:
A free day in mid-July, with the forest training camp ahead. Class 1-B rides into Musutafu to shop at Kiyashi Shopping Mall on a day of its own, and the Main Atrium swallows twenty people in under a minute. Itsuka Kendo holds the list: hiking boots, a rain shell, insect repellent, a flashlight, a week of socks, and a meeting time at the fountain she repeats three times.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: the class scatters. Setsuna Tokage splits into pieces to cover the Fashion Floors all at once and reports prices from four shops in one breath, until a security guard asks why a hand is floating by the sunglasses. Pony Tsunotori hunts for boots that fit hooves and wants a cowboy hat for the mountains. Kinoko Komori asks the staff how humid the camp will be and buys three rain hats. Yui Kodai shrinks the class's purchases until they fit in one tote bag. Tetsutetsu Tetsutetsu heads straight for the Food Court and anything with iron in it. Neito Monoma demands to know what Class 1-A bought and buys one more of each item. Ibara Shiozaki finds the music, the screens and the crowds hard to bear and stays near the fountain, praying quietly; she will not say she wants to leave.

The party can shop with any group, help Pony find boots, keep Tokage out of trouble with security, or notice Shiozaki and find her a quieter floor, for which she thanks the party gravely. If Class 1-A's lockdown at this mall has already happened, police stand at the entrances and the class talks about it in low voices; this day stays ordinary and no villain appears. A party that stayed at U.A. Academy meets the class at the Campus Bus Terminal on its way back, loaded with bags, and can help Kendo check the list.

The event is complete when the class meets at the fountain with everything on the list and heads home, or the party leaves.

b1_test_of_courage.title: The Test of Courage Night
b1_test_of_courage.beats:
The second night of the forest training camp, at the Wild Wild Pussycats Lodge. A brutal day of Quirk drills is over, both classes cooked their own curry at the Outdoor Kitchen and ate it under the trees, and at dinner Pixie-Bob announced the treat for tomorrow night: a test of courage in Beast's Forest, Class 1-A walking a dark route in pairs while Class 1-B does the scaring. Class 1-B has taken over a corner of the Lodge Hall to plan. Through the windows there is only forest and a clear, starry sky.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Neito Monoma has drawn the route from memory and built a plan with stations, timings and a script. Kinoko Komori is thrilled with the damp and promises mushrooms on every trunk at the turn. Reiko Yanagi will float a lantern a few steps behind each pair and let it go out. Shihai Kuroiro will rise out of the black between the trees, and rehearses his line twice until someone laughs and he mumbles the third. Manga Fukidashi tests which sound effect makes the best scare, very quietly for once. Yui Kodai has a small doll to enlarge at the right moment. Itsuka Kendo sets the one rule: scare them, never touch them, and nobody leaves the path. Monoma wants a station so frightening that 1-A will talk about it for the rest of the year; Kendo trims it down, and he sulks for a full minute.

The party can write a scare, rehearse one on a classmate, argue Monoma down or egg him on, or step out to the Training Clearing, where Vlad King and Tiger are laying out gear for the dawn drills; Vlad King looks the plan over, approves it loudly and orders everyone to bed early. The night stays calm: crickets, a cool wind, laughter from the 1-A side of the lodge.

The event is complete when the plan is set and Vlad King sends 1-B to the bunk rooms, or the party leaves.

b1_license_prep.title: License Exam Prep
b1_license_prep.beats:
The last days before the provisional license exam, at U.A. Academy under the lockdown that has held since the summer. Class 1-B will sit the exam on the same day as Class 1-A at a different venue, and nobody knows the format: only that the Hero Public Safety Commission runs it and that many examinees fail every year. Vlad King has booked the Main Gymnasium for 1-B's special-move drills, and at the end of each session he hands the floor to Itsuka Kendo.

Default course, as pressure the player can change: Kendo's point is simple. The whole country watched 1-B's Quirks on the Sports Festival broadcast, so other schools will have studied them; the class that stays together is the class that passes. On the whiteboard she builds pairs and trios and who covers whom: Yui Kodai's barriers behind Tetsutetsu Tetsutetsu's charge, Juzo Honenuki's mud in front of Setsuna Tokage's scouting pieces, Yosetsu Awase anchoring anything that moves. Neito Monoma wants the opposite, ambush teams that pick off the schools coming for them, and Tetsutetsu wants to charge whatever is closest. The argument gets loud, and Kendo lets it, then asks Monoma to plan inside her structure instead of around it. Vlad King roars approval at the end of every drill and pretends he is not nervous.
